findings.description: The inline policy grants full wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", giving the service user near-administrative control over compute, storage, and serverless resources. Compromise of this user's credentials would allow data exfiltration from any S3 bucket and arbitrary EC2/Lambda execution.

A permanent IAM access key is created for the user with no PGP key specified, so the secret is stored unencrypted in Terraform state and never rotates. Static long-lived keys attached to a highly privileged user are a prime credential-theft target; IAM roles with temporary credentials should be used instead.
Because no pgp_key is set, the access key's plaintext secret is written to Terraform state, making anyone with state-file read access able to authenticate as this privileged user.
The output svc_deploy_key_material publishes the access key secret material without marking it sensitive, so it is printed to the console and CI logs on every apply and readable via terraform output.

A long-lived IAM user with force_destroy enabled and attached wildcard permissions is used for deployment automation; there is no MFA or permissions boundary constraining it, widening the blast radius of credential compromise.
